newsitem.title: UK: UK soccer match arrests down by a third.
newsitem.headline: UK soccer match arrests down by a third.

text.p: Arrests at British soccer matches have fallen by a third over the past four years thanks to better police intelligence and bright modernised stadiums which are more welcoming to families, figures released on Wednesday showed.

The National Criminal Intelligence Service said the number of soccer-related arrests was 4,400 last football season, compared to 6,327 in 1992/93, despite attendance at matches rising to over 26 million.
But a senior police officer warned that gangs still represented a serious threat to the national game, whose reputation was badly tarnished in the late 1980s by hooliganism at home and in Europe.
"Developing good-quality intelligence on these criminals remains the key to stifling their attempts to cause trouble," Detective Superintendent Bryan Drew told a news conference.
"Intelligence allows us to concentrate our policing where it is most needed: to frustrate the activities of the troublemakers and to allow genuine fans to enjoy their football," he said.
Over the past 10 years, closed circuit television screens have been introduced at most grounds and soccer clubs have introduced all-seater stadiums in a bid to encourage families.
The 1996 European Championships in England passed off without major trouble from British fans.
The Football Association said the fall in arrests was "very encouraging".
"It is a tribute to the work of the police but also to the modern stadiums which are more welcoming for people," an FA spokesman said.
"But we are not complacent and it is vital that no one drops their guard. It would be foolish to say that the problem has gone away."
